questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Naming convention for libraries with -l
questions.q: If you want to link the libmath.so (or libmath.a) library, which parameter should be passed to the GCC compiler?
questions.hint: The -l flag automatically prepends the lib prefix and appends .so/.a extensions.
options: -lmath
-llibmath
-lmath.so
-Lmath
explanations: Correct! The `-l` flag drops the standard `lib` prefix and `.so`/`.a` extension. Therefore, for `libmath.so`, the `-lmath` flag is used.
Incorrect. The `lib` prefix does not need to be specified — `-llibmath` will look for a file named `liblibmath.so`.
Incorrect. The `.so` extension does not need to be written; the linker will select `.so` or `.a` on its own.
Incorrect. The `-L` flag specifies the path to the directory containing libraries, not the library name.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Order of -l flags during build
questions.q: Why might Command A fail with an 'undefined reference to...' error, while Command B compiles successfully?
questions.hint: The GCC linker (GNU ld) processes object files and libraries strictly from left to right.
options: The linker searches for unresolved symbols from left to right: if the `-l` library comes BEFORE the `.c`/`.o` file, unused symbols from it are discarded
According to the Linux standard, the `-lmath` flag must always be placed before `main.c`
This is a bug in a specific version of GCC
Flags with `-o` do not work if `-l` is at the beginning
explanations: Correct! `ld` scans files from left to right. When it sees `-lmath` right at the start, it doesn't yet have a list of unresolved functions from `main.c`, so it drops the library's functions as unnecessary. `-l` flags must always come AFTER the files that depend on them!
Incorrect. On the contrary, the `-l` flag must be placed AFTER the source code files.
Incorrect. This is a fundamental operating principle of classic linkers in UNIX/Linux.
Incorrect. The position of `-o app` does not affect the order of symbol resolution.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — libdl library and the -ldl flag
questions.q: Why is it mandatory to add the -ldl flag when compiling a program that uses dlopen(), dlsym(), or dlclose()?
questions.hint: Think about which specific Linux library implements these dynamic loading functions.
options: The dynamic loader API functions reside in a separate libdl.so library (in older glibc versions)
The -ldl flag is included to compress the executable file
The -ldl flag allows the use of the gdb debugger
This flag is used for compiling exclusively for 64-bit architectures
explanations: Correct! In Linux (prior to glibc 2.34), dynamic library management functions (`dlopen`, `dlsym`, `dlerror`, `dlclose`) resided in a separate `libdl.so` library, which needed to be explicitly linked via `-ldl`.
Incorrect. `libdl` has nothing to do with file compression.
Incorrect. The `-g` flag is used to enable debugging.
Incorrect. `libdl` is used regardless of the system's bitness.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Dynamic library lookup in dlopen
questions.q: Why will dlopen("libplugin.so", RTLD_LAZY) return NULL, even if libplugin.so is located in the current project directory?
questions.hint: Does the Linux dynamic loader search for libraries in the current working directory by default?
options: For security reasons, Linux by default does not search for libraries in the current folder '.' unless specified with './' or set in LD_LIBRARY_PATH / RPATH
dlopen accepts only absolute paths starting from root /
The RTLD_LAZY flag prohibits loading local files
The filename must specify the version (e.g., libplugin.so.1)
explanations: Correct! The Linux loader (`ld.so`) does not include the current folder `.` in the standard library search path. You must either explicitly write `"./libplugin.so"` or add the directory to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` / `rpath`.
Incorrect. Relative paths like `./libplugin.so` work perfectly.
Incorrect. `RTLD_LAZY` only determines when symbol binding occurs (as they are called).
Incorrect. The filename can be any valid path.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Position-Independent Code (-fPIC)
questions.q: Why is the -fPIC flag used when compiling source files into a dynamic library (.so)?
questions.hint: The acronym PIC stands for Position Independent Code.
options: Generates position-independent code, allowing the .so to be loaded at any virtual memory address without relocation
Accelerates floating-point calculations (Floating Point Instruction Controller)
Defines the maximum memory size for a shared library
Packs multiple files into a single .a archive
explanations: Correct! `-fPIC` (Position-Independent Code) generates assembly instructions using relative addressing. This allows multiple processes to map the same `.so` library at different virtual addresses in memory.
Incorrect. PIC is completely unrelated to floating-point calculations.
Incorrect. The flag does not limit memory size.
Incorrect. Packing files into `.a` archives is handled by the `ar` utility.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Creating shared libraries
questions.q: Which GCC flag tells the linker to create a shared object (.so) instead of a standard executable?
questions.hint: This option tells the compiler to build a Shared Library.
options: -shared
-static
-dynamic
-so
explanations: Correct! The `-shared` flag instructs GCC to create a dynamic/shared library (`.so`).
Incorrect. `-static` creates a statically linked executable with no external `.so` dependencies.
Incorrect. The `-dynamic` flag does not exist in GCC basic options for this purpose.
Incorrect. The `-so` flag does not exist.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Difference between -I and -L
questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between the compilation flags -I and -L?
questions.hint: One is for the preprocessing stage, the other is for the linking stage.
options: -I specifies the header file (.h) search directory, while -L specifies the library (.so / .a) search directory
-I specifies library directories, while -L specifies header file directories
-I is used for C++, while -L is used only for C language
-I links libraries dynamically, while -L links statically
explanations: Correct! `-I` (Include) adds a directory to the `#include <...>` search list, while `-L` (Link path) adds a directory to the library search path for the `-l` flag.
Incorrect. The flag meanings are swapped.
Incorrect. Both flags work identically for C and C++.
Incorrect. The flags specify directory paths, not the linkage type.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — LD_LIBRARY_PATH variable and RPATH
questions.q: What happens if you run a compiled program that requires a non-standard libcustom.so without setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH or RPATH?
questions.hint: What does the dynamic linker ld.so do during application launch?
options: Runtime error: error while loading shared libraries... No such file or directory
The program will automatically find .so in the current folder
The program will not compile at all
The system will automatically download libcustom.so from the internet
explanations: Correct! The dynamic loader `ld.so` won't find the library file in standard `/lib` or `/usr/lib` locations at startup and will crash with a shared library loading error.
Incorrect. The current directory is not searched by default.
Incorrect. Compilation and linking succeeded during the build phase (since `-L` was provided); the error occurs *at runtime*.
Incorrect. Linux OS does not automatically download missing libraries when launching a binary.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Compilation stage flags (-E, -S, -c)
questions.q: What does the command gcc -E main.c > main.i do?
questions.hint: Think about the very first processing stage GCC performs on a file.
options: Stops processing after the preprocessing stage (macro expansion, #include) and outputs the result
Generates a file with assembly code
Creates a finished object file main.i
Runs the syntax analyzer without saving the file
explanations: Correct! The `-E` flag forces GCC to run only the preprocessor (expand `#define`, substitute `#include` directives, strip comments) and direct output to stdout.
Incorrect. Generating assembly code is done via the `-S` flag.
Incorrect. An object file is created with the `-c` flag.
Incorrect. Output is saved to a file via `>` redirection.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Passing macros via command line (-D)
questions.q: What does the parameter -DBUFFER_SIZE=1024 do in a GCC command?
questions.hint: The letter D stands for Define.
options: Equivalent to declaring #define BUFFER_SIZE 1024 in all compiled files
Enables Debug mode with level 1024
Sets the maximum stack size to 1024 bytes
Sets the memory buffer size for the GCC compiler itself
explanations: Correct! The `-DNAME=VALUE` flag injects a preprocessor macro definition as if `#define NAME VALUE` were written at the top of the source file.
Incorrect. Debug mode is enabled using the `-g` flag.
Incorrect. Stack size is controlled by the linker and system limits.
Incorrect. This is not a compiler buffer setting.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Creating static libraries (.a)
questions.q: Which command line utility is used in Linux to bundle .o files into a static library (.a)?
questions.hint: An archiver for objects in .a format.
options: ar
ld
make
tar
explanations: Correct! The `ar` (archiver) utility is used to package multiple `.o` object files into a single `.a` static library file (e.g., `ar rcs libfoo.a foo.o bar.o`).
Incorrect. `ld` is the linker; it links executable files and `.so`.
Incorrect. `make` is a build automation system.
Incorrect. `tar` is a general-purpose file archiver.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — The -Wall flag (Trick question!)
questions.q: Is it true that the -Wall flag enables absolutely ALL possible compiler warnings in GCC?
questions.hint: Pay attention to the names of flags like -Wextra and -Wpedantic.
options: False (The name is misleading: -Wall only enables a recommended majority of warnings, but not all!)
True (-Wall stands for 'Warning All' and catches 100% of questionable code)
explanations: Correct! Despite its name, `-Wall` only includes the most popular base set of warnings. To enable additional checks, flags like `-Wextra`, `-Wpedantic`, `-Wconversion`, etc., are required.
Incorrect. The `-Wall` flag does not enable ALL existing warnings in GCC.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Specifics of the dlerror() function
questions.q: What will the second call printf("2: %s\n", dlerror()); output in this code snippet?
questions.hint: The dlerror() function has a specific side effect each time it is read.
options: 2: (null)
2: No such file or directory (duplicate of the first error)
Segmentation Fault
2: Error cleared
explanations: Correct! Calling `dlerror()` returns the current error string and RESETS it to NULL. A second call to `dlerror()`, provided no new loading errors occurred in between, is guaranteed to return `NULL` (printing `(null)`).
Incorrect. The error text is not preserved after the first read.
Incorrect. `printf` with `%s` safely handles `NULL` in glibc, printing `(null)`.
Incorrect. The message string is not replaced with "Error cleared".

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Constructors in shared libraries
questions.q: When will a function init_lib(), marked with the constructor attribute in a dynamic library, execute?
questions.hint: A special GCC attribute triggers automatically upon loading the module into memory.
options: Automatically upon loading the .so library into memory (via dlopen or when starting the program)
Only when unloading the library via dlclose()
Only upon an explicit call in main()
Upon the first access to any library variable
explanations: Correct! Functions with `__attribute__((constructor))` are automatically called by the dynamic loader right after mapping the `.so` into memory (during `dlopen` or at program startup).
Incorrect. For unloading, `__attribute__((destructor))` is used.
Incorrect. The function is called before executing the code that requested the library.
Incorrect. Execution occurs when loading the code, not when accessing data.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Passing parameters to the linker via -Wl
questions.q: What is the -Wl, prefix used for (e.g., -Wl,-rpath,/usr/local/lib) in GCC commands?
questions.hint: The letters Wl stand for Warning/Write to Linker.
options: To pass comma-separated options directly to the linker (ld)
To suppress linker warnings
To enable logging of the build process to a file
For static linking of individual modules
explanations: Correct! The `-Wl,option1,option2` prefix informs the GCC compiler driver to pass these parameters unchanged to the linker utility `ld`.
Incorrect. Suppressing warnings is done with the `-w` flag.
Incorrect. This is not a logging flag.
Incorrect. Linkage type is set via `-static` / `-shared` flags.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Exporting executable symbols (-rdynamic)
questions.q: Which flag must be passed to GCC when building an executable so that dlopen(NULL, ...) can locate functions from the main binary itself?
questions.hint: By default, an executable file does not place its symbols into the dynamic symbol table.
options: -rdynamic
-fPIC
-ldl
-export-all
explanations: Correct! The `-rdynamic` flag (or `-Wl,--export-dynamic`) forces the linker to add all global symbols of the executable to the dynamic symbol table. Without this, `dlsym(dlopen(NULL, ...), "func")` will return NULL.
Incorrect. `-fPIC` generates position-independent code but doesn't add symbols of the main file to the dynamic symbol table.
Incorrect. `-ldl` only links the loader API.
Incorrect. The `-export-all` flag does not exist in GCC for ELF systems.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Difference between -std=c11 and -std=gnu11
questions.q: What is the main difference between -std=c11 and -std=gnu11 flags in the GCC compiler?
questions.hint: One is strictly restricted by ISO standard, while the second includes GNU extensions.
options: -std=gnu11 enables GNU extensions and POSIX functions (popen, strdup, etc.), while -std=c11 disables them for strict ISO C compliance
-std=c11 is designed only for 32-bit systems
-std=gnu11 disables compiler optimizations
They are completely identical and synonyms
explanations: Correct! By default GCC uses the `gnuXX` dialect (e.g., `gnu11`), which includes language extensions and POSIX macro declarations. The `c11` flag enables strict ISO C standard compliance mode.
Incorrect. Both flags work on all supported architectures.
Incorrect. Language standard choice does not disable the optimizer.
Incorrect. Differences lie in available system headers and syntax extensions.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Default output filename
questions.q: What will the compiled file be named when calling gcc main.c without specifying the -o parameter?
questions.hint: This is the historical default output filename in UNIX systems (Assembler Output).
options: a.out
main.o
main
main.exe
explanations: Correct! For historical reasons, UNIX compilers in the absence of `-o <name>` save the finished executable file under the name `a.out`.
Incorrect. The `.o` file is created only when `-c` is present.
Incorrect. The compiler does not automatically take the source file name for the binary.
Incorrect. The `.exe` extension is used on Windows OS.

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Stopping compilation at assembly (-S)
questions.q: What extension will the file generated by gcc -S main.c have?
questions.hint: The -S flag stops the build after generating text assembly code.
options: .s
.o
.i
.so
explanations: Correct! The `-S` flag forces GCC to translate C code into assembly text and save the result in a file with a `.s` extension (e.g., `main.s`).
Incorrect. The `.o` extension is for binary object files (`-c` flag).
Incorrect. The `.i` extension is for post-preprocessor files (`-E` flag).
Incorrect. The `.so` extension is for shared libraries (`-shared` flag).

questions.topic: GCC / Linux — Combining -g and -O3
questions.q: What will happen if you invoke GCC with both gcc -g -O3 main.c flags specified simultaneously?
questions.hint: Debugging info stores links to source code lines, but the optimizer can reorder instructions.
options: The code will compile successfully with maximum optimization and will contain debug symbols, though step-by-step debugging may be difficult
The compiler will fail with an error due to flag incompatibility
The -O3 flag will completely disable the effect of the -g flag
The -g flag will automatically reset the optimization level to -O0
explanations: Correct! In GCC, debug info (`-g`) and optimization (`-O3`) are independent. You get an optimized binary with DWARF debug symbols, but due to inlining and instruction reordering, stepping through lines in GDB may 'jump'.
Incorrect. The flags are fully compatible.
Incorrect. Debug symbols will still be included in the binary.
Incorrect. Optimization level remains `-O3`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Stream redirection order
questions.q: Where will the error stream (stderr) be directed when executing this command?
questions.hint: Redirections in the Bash command line are processed strictly from left to right.
options: To the terminal (stdout up to the point of redirection)
To the output.txt file
To /dev/null
Will terminate with a syntax error
explanations: Correct! `2>&1` redirects stderr to wherever stdout points AT THAT MOMENT (the terminal). Only then does `> output.txt` send stdout to a file, but stderr remains tied to the terminal!
Incorrect. To redirect errors to a file, the correct syntax is `> output.txt 2>&1`.
Incorrect. `2>&1` does not direct output to a black hole device.
Incorrect. The syntax is completely valid.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Pipeline return code ($?)
questions.q: What will echo $? output by default in Bash if cat fails with an error (1) and grep succeeds and finds a match (0)?
questions.hint: By default, the $? variable holds the return code of only one command in the pipeline.
options: 0 (Return code of the last command in the pipeline)
1 (Return code of the first error)
Execution error
explanations: Correct! The `$?` variable contains the return code of the LAST command in the chain (`grep`). To track errors of previous commands, use `${PIPESTATUS[@]}` or `set -o pipefail`.
Incorrect. The `cat` error is overridden by the successful `grep` status.
Incorrect. Code 127 occurs when a command is missing.
Incorrect. The command returns a valid numeric value.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Special character handling and NUL delimiter
questions.q: Why are the -print0 flag in find and -0 in xargs needed when processing files?
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a filename contains spaces or newlines.
options: For safe handling of filenames containing spaces and newlines (uses a NUL byte instead of space)
For instant deletion without confirmation in 0 seconds
For running operations as superuser (root)
For creating backups of deleted files
explanations: Correct! Standard `xargs` splits input stream by spaces and newlines. Using `-print0` and `-0` sets the delimiter to a null byte (`\0`), allowing safe handling of any unusual filenames.
Incorrect. The `-0` flag sets a byte delimiter, not a timer.
Incorrect. Access permissions strictly depend on the current user.
Incorrect. These utilities do not automatically back up files.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Uncatchable process signals
questions.q: Can the SIGKILL (9) signal be caught or ignored inside a C program using signal() or sigaction()?
questions.hint: One of the Linux signals is designed to guarantee process termination by the kernel.
options: False (SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored — handling is performed by the OS kernel)
True (Any signal can be caught in a C program)
explanations: Correct! `SIGKILL` (9) and `SIGSTOP` signals cannot be caught or ignored. The kernel immediately terminates (or stops) the process.
Incorrect. Unlike `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT`, `SIGKILL` cannot be handled.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — strace tool
questions.q: What exactly does the strace console utility monitor when running a C program?
questions.hint: The letters st stand for System Trace.
options: System calls of a process to the Linux kernel and signals
Calls to C library functions (printf, malloc, etc.)
RAM memory leaks
Number of text lines in a file
explanations: Correct! `strace` intercepts and displays system calls (`open`, `read`, `write`, `mmap`, etc.) that the program makes to the OS kernel.
Incorrect. User library function calls are tracked by `ltrace`.
Incorrect. Finding memory leaks is done by `valgrind`.
Incorrect. Text lines are counted by `wc`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Difference between strace and ltrace
questions.q: What is the main difference between ltrace and strace utilities?
questions.hint: Pay attention to the first letter l (Library).
options: ltrace tracks dynamic library calls (Library calls), while strace tracks kernel system calls (System calls)
ltrace works only in a graphical interface
ltrace is used exclusively for debugging static libraries
They are completely identical utilities
explanations: Correct! `ltrace` (Library trace) traces calls to dynamic libraries (e.g., `printf`, `strcpy`), whereas `strace` monitors Linux kernel calls.
Incorrect. Both utilities work exclusively in the console.
Incorrect. Static libraries are not intercepted through PLT/GOT mechanisms of `ltrace`.
Incorrect. They have different call interception levels.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Enabling Core Dump files
questions.q: Why run ulimit -c unlimited before debugging a crashing C program?
questions.hint: By default in many distributions, core file size is limited to zero.
options: Removes the memory dump file (core dump) size limit upon program crash
Removes CPU usage limits
Prevents the program from crashing with a Segmentation Fault
Enables unlimited RAM allocation mode
explanations: Correct! The `ulimit -c unlimited` command allows the OS to save the memory image of a crashed process (`core dump`) of any size for subsequent debugging.
Incorrect. CPU time limits are regulated by `ulimit -t`.
Incorrect. Crashes due to invalid memory cannot be prevented by `ulimit`.
Incorrect. Virtual memory limit is set via the `-v` flag.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — One-time environment variables
questions.q: Will the VAR variable persist in the current Bash console environment after executing this command?
questions.hint: The VAR=val ./app syntax sets the variable only for the launched process.
options: False (The variable is passed ONLY to the child process ./app)
True (The variable will become available in the current session)
explanations: Correct! The declaration `VAR=10 ./app` places `VAR` into the environment of `./app` process only. It is not created or saved in the current Bash shell.
Incorrect. To keep the variable in the session, you must write `export VAR=10` on a separate line first.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — File wildcards (Globbing)
questions.q: Who expands the *.c wildcard into a list of filenames when running ./app *.c?
questions.hint: Does the C program itself receive the original asterisk in arguments?
options: The shell expands the wildcard BEFORE passing arguments to the program's argv
The C program itself inside the main() function
The GCC compiler during the build phase
The Linux kernel when loading the ELF file
explanations: Correct! In Linux, it is the `shell` (Bash) that matches files against `*.c` and passes the resulting list of files to `argv`. Unlike CMD/PowerShell on Windows, where expansion is performed by the application itself.
Incorrect. The C program receives an already expanded array of strings in `argv`.
Incorrect. GCC is not involved during execution in the terminal.
Incorrect. The kernel receives the formed `argv` array from `execve`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Memory bug hunting with Valgrind
questions.q: Which issues CANNOT be detected by the Valgrind Memcheck utility?
questions.hint: Valgrind tracks heap memory and dynamic arrays.
options: Overflow of a static array declared on the stack in C
Dynamic memory leaks (malloc without free)
Reading from uninitialized memory
Double free of a pointer
explanations: Correct! Basic `valgrind` (memcheck) catches heap errors, but CANNOT detect stack array out-of-bounds access! For stack checks, `AddressSanitizer` (`-fsanitize=address`) is better suited.
Incorrect. Memory leaks are a core target of `valgrind`.
Incorrect. Using uninitialized data is reported via `Uninitialised value`.
Incorrect. Repeated `free` calls are caught instantly.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Symbol analysis with nm
questions.q: What does the nm utility show with the -D flag?
questions.hint: The letter D points to the dynamic symbol table.
options: Dynamic symbols (functions and global variables) of a .so shared library
File dependencies in a Makefile
Size of debug information
Source code directories
explanations: Correct! The `nm` utility outputs the symbol table. The `-D` (or `--dynamic`) flag forces it to read the dynamic symbol table of a library/binary.
Incorrect. Dependencies in a Makefile are analyzed by `make`.
Incorrect. Debug information is inspected via `dwarfdump` or `gdb`.
Incorrect. The symbol table stores function and variable names.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Command isolation in Subshell
questions.q: Will the current working directory of your main console change after executing this command inside parentheses?
questions.hint: Parentheses ( ... ) run commands in a separate, isolated child process (Subshell).
options: False (The command executes in a subshell; the current directory of the main session remains unchanged)
True (The main console will switch to the /tmp folder)
explanations: Correct! Parentheses `( ... )` create a `subshell` (child process). All environment and directory changes inside the parentheses are lost when the subshell terminates.
Incorrect. Switching to `/tmp` occurs only within the child process.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — grep return codes
questions.q: What will echo $? output if grep finds no matches in a file?
questions.hint: Are the statuses 'found', 'not found', and 'file error' different?
options: 1 (If no matches are found)
0 (Successful execution)
2 (File access error)
explanations: Correct! `grep` returns `0` if a line is found, `1` if NO matches are found, and `2` on file reading or syntax errors.
Incorrect. 0 is returned only if the target text was found.
Incorrect. Code 2 indicates a fatal error (e.g., missing file).
Incorrect. Return codes in Linux cannot be negative (they range from 0 to 255).

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Pseudo-devices /dev/null and /dev/zero
questions.q: What is the difference between the pseudo-device /dev/zero and /dev/null?
questions.hint: Think about what happens when reading from these system files.
options: Reading from /dev/zero produces an infinite stream of null bytes (\0), while /dev/null immediately returns EOF (end of file)
/dev/null generates random numbers, while /dev/zero generates zeros
They are completely interchangeable
/dev/zero permanently deletes files without recovery
explanations: Correct! Reading from `/dev/zero` endlessly returns zero bytes (`\0`). Reading from `/dev/null` immediately returns 0 bytes (EOF). Writing to BOTH devices simply discards the data.
Incorrect. Random numbers are provided by `/dev/urandom` and `/dev/random`.
Incorrect. Their behavior upon reading is fundamentally different.
Incorrect. Writing to these files does not delete objects on disk.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Permissions and SUID bit
questions.q: What does the octal digit 4 mean in the permission mode chmod 4755 app?
questions.hint: This is the special SUID bit (Set User ID).
options: Sets the SUID bit: the program runs with the privileges of the file owner, not the user who launched it
Makes the file read-only
The file runs in debug mode
Prevents file deletion
explanations: Correct! The SUID flag (4 in the first octal position) forces the OS to run the binary with the file owner's privileges (e.g., `root` privileges, as in the `passwd` utility).
Incorrect. Read permission is represented by bit 4 in the standard rwx triad.
Incorrect. Debugging does not depend on permission flags.
Incorrect. Deletion prevention is configured via sticky bit or `chattr` attributes.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Post-mortem debugging in GDB
questions.q: Why is a core file (core dump) passed into the GDB debugger?
questions.hint: A core file contains a snapshot of the process RAM.
options: To analyze memory state, variables, and the call stack at the moment of the crash (post-mortem debugging)
To fix a bug directly in the executable file
To resume execution of the crashed program from the point of failure
For code optimization
explanations: Correct! The `core` file saves process memory at the time of a crash (Segmentation fault). GDB reads it and allows viewing the stack trace (`bt`), variable values, and the line of code that triggered the fault.
Incorrect. GDB does not edit C source code.
Incorrect. Resuming a crashed process from a core dump is impossible.
Incorrect. Core dump does not optimize calculations.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Viewing dependencies with ldd
questions.q: What will the command ldd ./app display for a compiled binary file?
questions.hint: ldd stands for List Dynamic Dependencies.
options: A list of all shared libraries (.so) required for the application to run, and their paths
The executable file size in bytes
A list of functions taking the longest time to run
The source C code of the application
explanations: Correct! `ldd` queries the dynamic loader and outputs a list of all `.so` libraries required to launch the program, along with their resolved locations.
Incorrect. File size is shown by `ls -l` or `du`.
Incorrect. Profiling is handled by `perf` or `gprof`.
Incorrect. `ldd` works only with compiled binary ELF files.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Process Substitution syntax
questions.q: What is the <(...) syntax called in Bash shell?
questions.hint: This construct allows passing command output where a file is expected.
options: Process Substitution
Command Substitution
Standard Input Redirection
Anonymous Pipe
explanations: Correct! The `<(command)` syntax is Process Substitution. It creates a named pipe (or `/dev/fd/X`) and allows utilities (such as `diff`) expecting files as parameters to read command output directly.
Incorrect. Command Substitution is `$(command)` or `` `command` ``.
Incorrect. Input redirection is written as `< file`.
Incorrect. A standard pipe is written as `|`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Analyzing ELF structure with readelf
questions.q: What information does the command readelf -h app show?
questions.hint: The -h flag stands for Header.
options: ELF Header (architecture, bitness, endianness, Entry Point address)
Headers of all functions in the C source code
Compilation history of the file
License information
explanations: Correct! `readelf -h` reads the main ELF file header and outputs metadata: target architecture (x86_64, ARM), file type (EXEC, DYN), `Entry point address`, and table sizes.
Incorrect. C source code is not present in compiled headers.
